newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel, PLO aim for Hebron announcement on Monday.
newsitem.headline: Israel, PLO aim for Hebron announcement on Monday.

text.p: Israel and the PLO discussed the final touches on a Hebron deal on Monday and an aide to Yasser Arafat promised an important announcement after mediation by the king of Jordan removed a key negotiating block.

Both sides said peacemakers, meeting at a Jerusalem hotel, could conclude a deal within hours, thanks to the compromise reached on Sunday for Israel to complete three troop withdrawals from other occupied West Bank areas by mid-1998.

An Israeli handover of 80 percent of Hebron has seemed within reach several times in recent months but concerns for the security of the West Bank town's 400 Jews and 100,000 Arabs -- along with other issues -- have delayed an agreement.

Arafat's adviser Nabil Abu Rdainah said the Palestinian leader would summon his cabinet and the PLO executive committee at 1700 GMT. "There will be an important announcement after that," he said without elaborating.

"If no new demands are raised today and the issues which were settled remain settled...we can reach a conclusion today," Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's cabinet secretary Danny Naveh told reporters.
Arafat and Netanyahu would meet soon to sew up a deal, officials on both sides said.
News of an imminent agreement angered members of Netanyahu's right-leaning cabinet and Jewish settler leaders who want to hold on to the lands occupied since a 1967 war.
At least seven ministers on Netanyahu's 18-member cabinet were expected to oppose the deal.
Jewish settlers called an "emergency meeting" and warned that an Israeli withdrawal would lead to bloodshed.

"The agreement is liable to create an extremely severe and dangerous situation here," said Noam Arnon, spokesman for the Hebron settlers. The West Bank town has been a flashpoint for Arab-Israeli violence.
Outside the hotel where negotiators were meeting, about 20 Israelis waving black flags and Israeli flags held up signs including one that read: "Hebron deal spells end of Zionism."
U.S. peace envoy Dennis Ross, buoyed by the progress during a lightning visit of Jordan's King Hussein, cancelled plans to head home after a three-week mediation effort.

A timeframe for the West Bank pullbacks, originally due to be completed by September this year, had been the main stumbling block to a deal on Hebron, a town holy to Moslems and Jews as the biblical Abraham's burial place.
The PLO had been reluctant to sign an accord without a commitment from Israel to carry out the additional West Bank pullbacks agreed in previous peace deals.

Israel proposed completing the West Bank pullbacks by May 1999 and the United States suggested 1998. The PLO demanded Israel stick to the timetable signed by Israel's previous left-leaning government in 1995.
Under the compromise, proposed by Egypt and Jordan and pushed by the king on Sunday, the withdrawals will be completed by sometime in mid-1998, PLO officials said.
In Cairo on Monday, Jordan's Prime Minister Abdul-Karim al-Kabariti briefed Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak on the compromise.
